You are extracting load-bearing passages from one chapter of a guitar method book.

The user will give you the verbatim text of one chapter. Extract every passage
that does any of the following:

- teaches a technique (how to play, fingering, hand position, picking pattern)
- defines a concept (a chord type, a scale, a position system, a terminology)
- gives a rule (when to do X, what to avoid, what to prefer)
- shows a load-bearing example (an exercise that illustrates a method's
  characteristic move)

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  { "quotes": [
      { "topic": "<short topic label>",
        "verbatim_quote": "<exact substring of the input>",
        "why_load_bearing": "<one sentence on why this passage matters>",
        "page": <int, optional>
      },
      ...
  ] }

CRITICAL RULES:
1. `verbatim_quote` MUST be an EXACT substring of the input text. Do not
   paraphrase. Do not add words. Do not fix typos. Copy character-for-character.
2. If you can't find a substantial passage in the input that fits a topic,
   skip the topic — don't fabricate.
3. Skip prose that is purely biographical, motivational, or transitional.
   Keep prose that teaches.
4. Aim for 3-15 quotes per chapter. A chapter with only one load-bearing
   passage gets one quote; a dense chapter gets many.
5. `topic` is a short label (2-6 words). Use the book's own terminology
   when possible.
6. `why_load_bearing` is one sentence in YOUR voice explaining the
   significance — not a paraphrase of the quote.

  The Secret of the Two Chords
  As mentioned before, the natural major scale is one of the 5irst subjects we must study to
  start improvising. It can summarize the whole harmonic 5ield into one scale. However, the
  avoid note (perfect 4th) can create some melodic problems, especially over the root chord
  and the relative minor chord (Cmaj7 and Am7 in the key of “C”).

  However this scale works perfectly when played over Dm7 (Dorian), Em7 (Phrygian), Fmaj7
  (Lydian), G7 (mixolydian), Bø (locrian), even while using the avoid note. We must be
  careful with our note choices. For example over a G7 chord, we should not stop on a "C"
  note. The only exception for this would be when we have a Gsus7 chord, because in this
  case the “C” is a chord tone and it will work perfectly.

  But for now, let’s concentrate on two chords: Cmaj7 and Am7, ignoring for a moment the
  rest of the chords from the harmonic 5ield. In order to solve the avoid note issue, we will
  not use it for the time being. Therefore, we will create melodies for Cmaj7 that can 5it over
  Ionian or Lydian chords, and melodies for Am7 that can 5it over Dorian or Aeolian chords.
  This is the beginning of what we will call “The Secret of the 2 Chords”.
                               68


  As mentioned before, it is not enough to only use the scales of the chords to create
  melodies, we must add stronger melodic structures to them such as triads and tetrads . As
  we will not be using the avoid note (F) over Cmaj7 and Am7, we will discard all the triads
                      46




  and tetrads that contain an "F" note (4th degree). See the remaining chords below:


  • Tetrads: Cmaj7, Em7, Am7

  • Triads: C, Em, G, Am


  I bet you are asking yourself what about the other chords of the harmonic 5ield, how can
  we just forget them? Later on, we will use the major 7 lines and minor 7th lines over other
  chords, creating the sound of the modes without thinking about them, just like we did
  using the harmonic 5ield chords over a continuous bass note. But for now let’s focus in
  “Major 7th and Minor 7th chords”.

  Chord Superimposition (Chord Stacking)
                                                                                                 4668




  The word superimpose means to join, add, propose an idea or concept based on another
  existing idea. In music, it means using more than one chord simultaneously in a melodic or
  harmonic form. Harmonically, it is the joining of two or more chords forming a single chord.
  Melodically it is to play notes from two or more different chords over a determined chord.
  The superimposition is a simpler and more melodic way of using the notes of a scale,
  without thinking of them as single notes, but as part of a pre established melodic structure
  such as triades and tetrads. John Coltrane used to call this: “chord stacking".
  It is important to understand that superimposed chords or stacking chords only works
  using triads and tetrads for a simple reason, the tensions are created by the mixture of two
  or more chords, so there is no need to use extended possibilities.




  “Chord Stacking” Examples:
  If we play Gmaj7 (G, B, D, F# ) over the Cmaj7, we would have a “C “ Lydian sound
  melodically, and a Lydian chord harmonically. However it is difHicult to play these
  superimposed chords correctly on the guitar. The only instrument that can apply this
  harmonic concept correctly is the piano. To achieve this on the guitar, we must arpeggiate
  two chords, one after the other, forming one chord. We call these: "block chords".
  The best way to understand the superimposed chords is through chord arpeggios.

Octave displacement is a musical term that describes the changing of direction of a scale
line, in other words, it describes when a scale line changes to a diffent octave. This
technique has been used since the Renaissance Period, more precisely in Baroque with the

But to clarify the idea let’s understand what counterpoint is. In music, this term refers to

relationship between each other. The starting point for counterpoint is the creation of a

melodies that will be the harmony part of the cantus formus.

There are many types of counterpoint with many different rules, and that will lead us to
what we call species counterpoint, a method that has been the basis for polyphonic music.
Each species of counterpoint has different rules and the melodies must follow them in
relation to the cantus Eirmus.

So, among many techniques of how to create melodies with a harmonic relationship
between each other, the octave displacement is one of the most useful, and it may help the

let's be clear why we are not using inverted tetrads. First of all, it is important to understand that

the reason why the strongest chord construction we have in western harmony are:


1) Tertian Chords: built from superimposed 3rds;

2) Quartal Chords: built from superimposed 4ths.

Applying Quartal Melodic Ideas                                                                                                                                      4668




The quartal melodic ideas are melodies using consecutive 4ths, forming many "sus chords".
This type of approach is very important not only to create melodies, but for harmony.
However, in this book we will cover only some melodic examples that will be connected
with the scale arpeggios and also common arpeggios.

It is important to mention that we will not use quartal ideas containing the major scale
avoid note 4th, just like we did with arpeggios and scale arpeggios. Therefore, we can
have the possibilities below to build our melodies:

1) D, G, C                       3) A, D, G

2) E, A , D                      4) B, E, A

Note: We will study the inverted quartal triads later in the next GBI Books. For now,
enjoy the melodies formed by consecutive 4ths (Quartal Triad 3rd Inversion).

  Creating “Out Side Ideas”                                                                       4668




  It is important to emphasize again, that the “secret of the two chords” is based on major 7th
  and minor 7th chord arpeggio ideas using some added notes, not scales. Therefore, in order
  to make it work, we must memorize some melodic lines, that as time goes by will be
  transformed and played differently every time we use them.
  In addition to creating the sound of the modes without playing scales, we can also use
  major 7th and minor 7th chord arpeggio ideas to create substitute harmonies, resulting in
  what we call “out side melodies”. When we do this, we add notes that do not belong to the
  preset harmony, but they work well because they create different colors over the chords,
  making the melodies become hybrid, and not predictable as lines that use one concept or a
  scale wise approach.
  In order to go deeper into the concept of the “secret of the two chords”, let’s learn how to
  apply it over dominant 7th chords that have the function of leading to other chords. Let’s
  use the altered chord as an example, because it has all the tension notes we need. We have
  Eive speciEic cases. (C#7alt chord as example below):

  • C#7alt → As we know an altered chord can be:
  a) C#7(#9)      b) C#7(b9)           c) C#7(#11)           d) C#7(b13)


  Attention:
  It is important to understand that this concept can be used over a static altered chord, or

  over any dominant 7th chord that has the function of leading to other chords. For example,
   we could use it over a C#7(b9)13 leading to F#maj7, or over a C#sus(b9) leading to F#m7 ,
  even knowing that these chords do not belong to the altered chord family.

           Minor 7th Chord half step above the Altered Chord

  and “pure” melodic lines. In addition to the connection between Dm7, G7 and C#7, we have
